title: 02. Networking, Protocols & APIs: WebSockets
summary: WebSocket is a full-duplex, bidirectional communication protocol that upgrades a single HTTP request into a persistent TCP connection over which client and server can exchange framed text or binary messages at any time,…

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** WebSocket is a full-duplex, bidirectional communication protocol that upgrades a single HTTP request into a persistent TCP connection over which client and server can exchange framed text or binary messages at any time, without the per-message HTTP overhead.
WebSockets were standardized in RFC 6455 (2011) to solve a problem that plain HTTP could not: server-initiated push. HTTP is strictly request-response — the client asks, the server answers, the connection closes. If a chat server wants to push a new message to a browser the instant it arrives, HTTP has no native way to do it; the client must keep asking ("anything new?"). WebSockets fix this with a two-step protocol. First, the client issues a normal HTTP GET request with the `Upgrade: websocket` and `Connection: Upgrade` headers plus a random `Sec-WebSocket-Key`. The server, if it speaks WebSockets, replies with HTTP `101 Switching Protocols`, a `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` value derived from the key (proving it understood the handshake), and from that point on the same TCP socket is no longer HTTP — it is a bidirectional frame-based wire protocol. Both sides may send opcode-tagged frames (text, binary, ping, pong, close) at any time, with very small per-frame overhead (2-14 bytes of header). Because the connection stays open, latency drops to a single TCP round trip per message instead of a fresh TLS+HTTP handshake every time, and the server can push data the moment it is produced instead of waiting for the next poll.

WebSockets matter because real-time UX is now table stakes. **WhatsApp** runs its real-time messaging on a WebSocket-based protocol layered over a single persistent connection per device — when your friend hits send, the server pushes the message to your phone over the existing socket within a few hundred milliseconds, without your phone having to poll. **Slack** uses WebSockets to deliver every typing indicator, message reaction, channel switch, and presence update live; opening the Slack web app immediately opens a WebSocket to `wss://wss-primary.slack.com`. **Discord** famously scaled WebSockets to roughly 5 million concurrent connections per gateway shard by switching from Python to Elixir/Erlang BEAM in 2020 — Elixir's lightweight processes map perfectly to one-process-per-connection, and BEAM's preemptive scheduling let them hold millions of idle sockets cheaply. **Zoom, Figma, Google Docs, and Notion** all use WebSockets (or a close variant) for collaborative cursors, voice/video signaling, and live document sync. The pattern is universal: any feature where the server must push to the client within sub-second latency — chat, multiplayer, live dashboards, collaborative editing, financial tickers — uses WebSockets.

A real-world example worth studying is **Discord's migration**. Their original Python + WebSockets stack handled about 70,000 concurrent connections per node before the GIL and per-connection memory cost became painful; they rewrote the gateway in Elixir and scaled to roughly 1,000,000 concurrent connections per node, then sharded the gateway across many nodes with a routing layer that maps each user to the correct shard. Behind the gateway, a Redis-backed pub/sub fan-out delivers each event to the right set of gateway nodes, which then push to the right set of WebSocket clients. **Slack** uses a similar pattern — its "gateway" is many stateful WebSocket servers, and a routing service ensures a user's events always reach the node holding their connection. The general scaling recipe is: sticky sessions at the load balancer (so a reconnecting client lands on the same node), Redis or Kafka pub/sub to fan out events to whichever node currently owns each recipient's socket, and heartbeat ping/pong frames to detect dead connections within seconds.

The trade-offs and pitfalls deserve attention. First, **state is sticky** — unlike stateless HTTP where any backend can serve any request, a WebSocket connection lives on one specific server. If that server dies, every client on it must reconnect (and the server must flush any in-flight messages or risk losing them). Load balancers must use sticky sessions or hash-based routing (by a `session_id` cookie or query param), which limits failover flexibility. Second, **connection cost** — each open socket consumes a file descriptor and roughly 50-100 KB of memory on the server (more for buffered queues); a million connections is roughly 50-100 GB of RAM just for sockets, plus the cost of the application state per connection. Third, **back-pressure and slow consumers** — if a server pushes 1000 messages/second to a client on a slow mobile network, the server's send buffer fills, kernel memory grows, and eventually the server must either drop messages, close the connection, or OOM. Robust WebSocket servers implement per-connection send queues with high-water marks that close or back off slow clients. Fourth, **no built-in reconnection or message ordering across reconnects** — if the connection drops mid-stream, the client must reconnect (the browser's `WebSocket` API does NOT auto-reconnect, unlike `EventSource`), and the application must implement resume logic (sequence numbers, replay buffers, `Last-Event-ID`-style cursors) to avoid losing or duplicating messages. Fifth, **proxies, firewalls, and corporate networks** — many proxies buffer HTTP responses, which breaks WebSocket frames; the handshake must use `Upgrade` headers that some intermediaries strip. Using TLS (`wss://`) on port 443 sidesteps most of these because intermediaries treat the connection as opaque encrypted traffic they cannot inspect or buffer. WebSockets connect to many other system design concepts: they sit on top of TCP (Phase 2 Topic 2) and TLS (Phase 2 Topic 5), they are the transport for chat in WhatsApp/Slack/Discord (Phase 6 message queues), scaling them out uses Redis/Kafka pub-sub fan-out (Phase 6 + Phase 8), and their back-pressure problems are an instance of the broader flow-control topic in Phase 7 reliability.

TCP connection closed ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------+ HTTP GET + Upgrade: websocket +----------------+ | Browser | --------------------------------> | WebSocket | | (ws client)| <------------------------------ | Server | +-----------+ HTTP 101 Switching Protocols +-------+--------+ | | | (TCP connection now speaks WebSocket) | | | | text frame "msg" -----------> | | binary frame [bytes]-----------> | | <--------- ping | | ----------> pong | | <--------- text "push!" | | | +-----------+ v-------+--------+ \ | Per-connection | \ close frame 1000 | state: user_id,| \---------> | subscriptions, | | send queue | +----------------+ Frame format (RFC 6455): +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+ |FIN|RSV|opcode|MASK| payload len (7/16/64 bits) | +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+ | masking key (4 bytes, client->server only) | +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+ | payload data ... | +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+ opcodes: 0x0 continuation, 0x1 text, 0x2 binary, 0x8 close, 0x9 ping, 0xA pong ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The browser opens a normal HTTP connection and sends a GET request carrying `Upgrade: websocket`, `Connection: Upgrade`, `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13`, and a randomly generated `Sec-WebSocket-Key` (16 bytes base64-encoded). The server concatenates this key with the magic GUID `258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11`, takes the SHA-1 hash, base64-encodes the result, and returns it as `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` in an HTTP `101 Switching Protocols` response. This proves the server actually understood the WebSocket protocol (not just a naive HTTP server echoing headers) and prevents cross-protocol attacks. From this byte forward, the TCP socket is no longer HTTP. 2. Both sides may now send WebSocket frames at any time. Each frame has a 2-14 byte header (FIN bit, opcode, mask bit, payload length, optional masking key) followed by the payload. Client-to-server frames must be XOR-masked with a 4-byte key (a defense against confused-deputy attacks on intermediaries); server-to-client frames are unmasked. `text` frames must be valid UTF-8; `binary` frames carry raw bytes. `ping` and `pong` frames are 0-125 byte control frames exchanged as heartbeats — the server pings every 30s, the client must pong back, and a missed pong within a few seconds signals a dead connection. `close` frames carry a status code (1000 normal closure, 1001 going away, 1006 abnormal closure, 1011 internal error) and an optional reason string; both sides exchange close frames before TCP teardown. 3. To scale beyond one server, a load balancer (HAProxy, NGINX, AWS ALB, Cloudflare) routes the initial HTTP Upgrade request to a backend, typically using sticky sessions or a hash of a session cookie so reconnecting clients land on the same node holding their state. When a server wants to push a message to user X whose socket lives on a different node, it publishes the event to a Redis/Kafka pub-sub channel; every WebSocket node subscribes, the node that owns user X's socket receives the event and writes it to the socket. Heartbeats (ping/pong every 30s, idle timeout 60s) keep the connection alive through NATs and detect dead sockets. Connection state — user_id, subscriptions, last-acknowledged sequence — lives in the node's memory plus a shared store (Redis) so a reconnecting client on a different node can resume.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- RFC 6455: SHA1(key + magic) then base64.
- Read one WebSocket frame from the socket.
- Send one WebSocket frame.
- Minimal WebSocket server + client in pure Python stdlib.
- Implements RFC 6455: HTTP Upgrade handshake, frame encode/decode
- (text, binary, ping, pong, close), masking, and a tiny chat demo.
- Frame encode/decode (RFC 6455)
- Echo loop: text -> UPPER, ping -> pong, close -> close.

**Defines:** `server_accept_key()`, `parse_request()`, `build_handshake_response()`, `recv_exact()`, `read_frame()`, `write_frame()`, `EchoServer`, `client_send_and_receive()`

```python
# Minimal WebSocket server + client in pure Python stdlib.
# Implements RFC 6455: HTTP Upgrade handshake, frame encode/decode
# (text, binary, ping, pong, close), masking, and a tiny chat demo.

import socket
import threading
import hashlib
import base64
import struct
import os
import time

MAGIC = "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11"

# --- Handshake (server side) ------------------------------------

def server_accept_key(client_key: str) -> str:
    """RFC 6455: SHA1(key + magic) then base64."""
    h = hashlib.sha1((client_key + MAGIC).encode()).digest()
    return base64.b64encode(h).decode()

def parse_request(req_bytes: bytes) -> dict:
    text = req_bytes.decode("latin-1")
    head, _, body = text.partition("\r\n\r\n")
    lines = head.split("\r\n")
    method, path, _ver = lines[0].split(" ", 2)
    headers = {}
    for line in lines[1:]:
        k, _, v = line.partition(":")
        headers[k.strip().lower()] = v.strip()
    return {"method": method, "path": path, "headers": headers}

def build_handshake_response(client_key: str) -> bytes:
    accept = server_accept_key(client_key)
    return (
        "HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\n"
        "Upgrade: websocket\r\n"
        "Connection: Upgrade\r\n"
        f"Sec-WebSocket-Accept: {accept}\r\n\r\n"
    ).encode()

# --- Frame encode/decode (RFC 6455) -----------------------------

def recv_exact(sock: socket.socket, n: int) -> bytes:
    buf = b""
    while len(buf) < n:
        chunk = sock.recv(n - len(buf))
        if not chunk:
            raise ConnectionError("socket closed mid-frame")
        buf += chunk
    return buf

def read_frame(sock: socket.socket) -> dict:
    """Read one WebSocket frame from the socket."""
    b1, b2 = recv_exact(sock, 2)
    fin = (b1 & 0x80) != 0
    opcode = b1 & 0x0F
    masked = (b2 & 0x80) != 0
    length = b2 & 0x7F
    if length == 126:
        length = struct.unpack(">H", recv_exact(sock, 2))[0]
    elif length == 127:
        length = struct.unpack(">Q", recv_exact(sock, 8))[0]
    mask = recv_exact(sock, 4) if masked else b""
    payload = recv_exact(sock, length) if length else b""
    if masked:
        payload = bytes(b ^ mask[i % 4] for i, b in enumerate(payload))
    return {"fin": fin, "opcode": opcode, "payload": payload}

def write_frame(sock: socket.socket, opcode: int, payload: bytes,
                mask: bool = False) -> None:
    """Send one WebSocket frame. Server->client is unmasked by spec."""
    header = bytearray()
    header.append(0x80 | opcode)  # FIN=1
    length = len(payload)
    mask_bit = 0x80 if mask else 0x00
    if length < 126:
        header.append(mask_bit | length)
    elif length < 65536:
        header.append(mask_bit | 126)
        header.extend(struct.pack(">H", length))
    else:
        header.append(mask_bit | 127)
        header.extend(struct.pack(">Q", length))
    if mask:
        mask_key = os.urandom(4)
        header.extend(mask_key)
        payload = bytes(b ^ mask_key[i % 4] for i, b in enumerate(payload))
    sock.sendall(bytes(header) + payload)

OP_TEXT, OP_BINARY, OP_CLOSE, OP_PING, OP_PONG = 0x1, 0x2, 0x8, 0x9, 0xA

# --- Server ----------------------------------------------------

class EchoServer:
    def __init__(self, host="127.0.0.1", port=8765):
        self.host, self.port = host, port
        self.sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
        self.sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)

    def serve(self):
        self.sock.bind((self.host, self.port))
        self.sock.listen(8)
        while True:
            conn, _ = self.sock.accept()
            threading.Thread(target=self._handle, args=(conn,),
                             daemon=True).start()

    def _handle(self, conn: socket.socket):
        try:
            req_bytes = conn.recv(4096)
            req = parse_request(req_bytes)
            assert req["headers"].get("upgrade") == "websocket"
            client_key = req["headers"]["sec-websocket-key"]
            conn.sendall(build_handshake_response(client_key))
            # Echo loop: text -> UPPER, ping -> pong, close -> close.
            while True:
                frame = read_frame(conn)
                if frame["opcode"] == OP_TEXT:
                    msg = frame["payload"].decode("utf-8")
                    reply = f"echo: {msg.upper()}".encode()
                    write_frame(conn, OP_TEXT, reply)
                elif frame["opcode"] == OP_PING:
                    write_frame(conn, OP_PONG, frame["payload"])
                elif frame["opcode"] == OP_CLOSE:
                    write_frame(conn, OP_CLOSE, b"\x03\xe8goodbye")
                    break
        except (ConnectionError, AssertionError, KeyError):
            pass
        finally:
            conn.close()

# --- Client ----------------------------------------------------

def client_send_and_receive(host, port, messages):
    s = socket.create_connection((host, port))
    key = base64.b64encode(os.urandom(16)).decode()
    req = (
        f"GET /chat HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {host}:{port}\r\n"
        "Upgrade: websocket\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\n"
        f"Sec-WebSocket-Key: {key}\r\n"
        "Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n\r\n"
    ).encode()
    s.sendall(req)
    resp = s.recv(4096)
    assert b"101 Switching Protocols" in resp, "handshake failed"
    assert server_accept_key(key).encode() in resp, "accept key mismatch"
    for msg in messages:
        write_frame(s, OP_TEXT, msg.encode(), mask=True)
        reply = read_frame(s)
        print(f"  client sent {msg!r} -> server replied "
              f"{reply['payload'].decode()!r}")
    write_frame(s, OP_CLOSE, b"\x03\xe8bye", mask=True)
    s.close()

# --- Demo -----------------------------------------------------

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== WebSocket demo (pure stdlib) ===\n")
    srv = EchoServer()
    threading.Thread(target=srv.serve, daemon=True).start()
    time.sleep(0.2)
    print("[server] listening on ws://127.0.0.1:8765\n")
    client_send_and_receive("127.0.0.1", 8765,
                            ["hello", "world", "ping me"])
    print("\n[client] connection closed cleanly")
```

quiz.question: What is a WebSocket, and how does it differ from HTTP?
options: Long polling** — client sends HTTP GET, server holds the request open up to 30s waiting for data, then responds; client immediately re-requests.
The masking key is included in the frame header in plaintext, so masking is NOT a security feature (anyone can unmask).
Text and binary are the data opcodes; close, ping, pong are control opcodes that must be processed even mid-fragmented-message.
Direction** — HTTP is strictly request-response (client asks, server answers); WebSocket is bidirectional (either side sends at any time).
quiz.explanation: Direction** — HTTP is strictly request-response (client asks, server answers); WebSocket is bidirectional (either side sends at any time). (2) Persistence — HTTP/1.1 typically closes or pools a request per resource; WebSocket is one long-lived connection. (3) Overhead — HTTP repeats headers on every request (~200-800 bytes); WebSocket frames are 2-14 bytes.

quiz.explanation: RFC 6455 defines six opcodes: 0x0 continuation (for fragmented messages), 0x1 text (UTF-8 payload), 0x2 binary (raw bytes), 0x8 close (carries status code + reason), 0x9 ping (control, 0-125 byte payload), 0xA pong (control, mirrors ping payload). Text and binary are the data opcodes; close, ping, pong are control opcodes that must be processed even mid-fragmented-message. Ping/pong matters for three reasons.

quiz.question: What is the masking requirement in WebSocket frames, and why does it exist?
options: Text and binary are the data opcodes; close, ping, pong are control opcodes that must be processed even mid-fragmented-message.
Long polling** — client sends HTTP GET, server holds the request open up to 30s waiting for data, then responds; client immediately re-requests.
Direction** — HTTP is strictly request-response (client asks, server answers); WebSocket is bidirectional (either side sends at any time).
The masking key is included in the frame header in plaintext, so masking is NOT a security feature (anyone can unmask).
quiz.explanation: RFC 6455 mandates that every frame sent from client to server MUST be XOR-masked with a 4-byte masking key (randomly generated per frame and included in the header). Server-to-client frames must NOT be masked. The masking key is included in the frame header in plaintext, so masking is NOT a security feature (anyone can unmask).
